articles.title: South Africa-Trump row: US limits visas for officials over alleged anti-white discrimination
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says South Africa has not addressed US concerns over racial inequality.
articles.body:
The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries.

The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers.

South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim.

"The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid ​out concerns," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the restrictions on Tuesday.

He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa."

Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions.

Ramaphosa struggles to mend fences with Trump

Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims?

Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution."

But the South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land.

South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that more white people have fallen victim to violent crime than other racial groups.

Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances.

The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court.

Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights.

The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures.

Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population.

In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States".

He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities.

"The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added.

He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law."

The South African government is yet to respond to the US restrictions.

The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations.

It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter."

South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House last May with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers.

But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited.

Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa.

The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests.

articles.title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
articles.summary: The US president has pushed the issue to the forefront of American politics - even at the risk of losing supporters.
articles.body:
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.

It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.

Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.

The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.

OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms

AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act

Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.

Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.

"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."

Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.

"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."

According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."

A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.

It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.

Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.

But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?

The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI

Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.

According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.

Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.

Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.

"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."

The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.

Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.

Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump

Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.

"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."

Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.

These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.

In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.

"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."

Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.

With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.

With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.

But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.

Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.

"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

articles.title: NEWT GINGRICH: Republicans can win the 2026 midterms — if they follow the plan
articles.summary: A five-part strategic framework outlines how Republicans can expand the House majority, win Senate races and build a broader coalition for 2026.
articles.body: Republicans can win the 2026 election. They can expand the House majority, win Senate races, strengthen Republican governors and state legislators, and build a much broader national majority. But victory will not happen automatically. REPUBLICANS NEED A REAGAN-STYLE VISION TO WIN THE BATTLE OVER AMERICA'S FUTURE Republicans have a bad habit of assuming that if Democrats are sufficiently unpopular, voters will simply turn to us. History does not work that way. Elections are won by parties that understand the choice, define the choice, and relentlessly communicate the choice. That is why I developed a five-part series on How to Win 2026. It is not intended simply as political commentary. It is a practical framework for Republican candidates, campaign staffs, activists, donors and voters who want to understand what must be done between now and Election Day. The first requirement is strategic clarity. There are always two political realities. One is the reality described every day by the Washington establishment, the national news media, consultants and conventional polling. The other is the deeper reality of what Americans actually believe and how they will behave when presented with a clear choice. Republicans must operate in the second reality. The great lesson of successful campaigns — from Ronald Reagan to the Contract with America to President Donald Trump — is simple: Win the argument, then win the vote (to borrow a phrase from British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher). VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY The second part of the plan is to make Democrats explain their own party. The Democratic Party is being steadily pulled toward a big government socialist ideology which is far more radical than most Americans understand. TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% Republicans should not exaggerate. They do not need to. Use Democrats’ own words. Use their votes. Use their proposals. Show voters what leading Democrats are actually saying about immigration, policing, government spending, taxation, energy, healthcare and the role of government. Then ask a simple question: Is this really what you want for America? The third part is to deal directly with the issues which affect people’s lives every day. SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT Affordability is real. Families feel it every time they go to the grocery store, pay rent, buy a house, visit a doctor or fill up their car. Republicans must describe the progress they’ve made to lower costs, grow the economy, create better-paying jobs and increase take-home pay. They must also talk about the things they’ve done which will help the economy in the future but need a little time to make an impact (such as attracting new manufacturing to the U.S.). Then, of course, they must explain what still needs to be done – and articulate their plan to do them. At the same time, we must communicate a serious strategy for dealing with Iran and the growing national security challenges facing the United States. You do not win elections by avoiding difficult issues. You win by solving them. The fourth part of the plan may be the most important. Republicans should become the American Party. This does not mean creating a new party. It means identifying the issues on which 70%, 80% and even 90% of Americans already agree — and making those issues central to the campaign. There are enormous majorities for common-sense positions on border security, voter identification, lower taxes, healthcare transparency, government accountability and other reforms. Why would Republicans allow themselves to be trapped inside a 50-50 political system when they can campaign on 70-30 issues? The fifth part is a positive vision for a healthier America. Healthcare gets its own section, because it is a matter of life and death for every American and makes up roughly one-fifth of the economy. The current health system is too expensive, too bureaucratic, and too often designed around institutions rather than patients. Republicans should champion price transparency, greater choice, stronger rural healthcare, direct primary care, new medical technologies and aggressive efforts to eliminate fraud and waste from Medicare and Medicaid. This is not simply a healthcare agenda. It is an opportunity to improve the lives of every American family. Taken together, these five parts form a roadmap for victory. Republican candidates should study it. Campaign managers should build messages around it. Activists should share it. Voters should use it to hold candidates accountable. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The choice in 2026 can be made remarkably clear: big-government socialism or free enterprise; higher costs or greater prosperity; ideological extremism or American common sense; bureaucratic healthcare or a healthier America. Republicans can win this argument. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If they win the argument, they can win the election. The plan is here. Now they must use it. articles.title: 7 biggest surprises from the 2026 primary cycle
articles.summary: The 2026 primary cycle has served up enough surprises to fill out a bingo card. Tuesday’s primaries in Delaware marked the last contests of the season, as both parties gear up for the battle for control of Congress Over the last six months, the left flank of the Democratic Party cemented its political power, ousting…
articles.body:
The 2026 primary cycle has served up enough surprises to fill out a bingo card.

Tuesday’s primaries in Delaware marked the last contests of the season, as both parties gear up for the battle for control of Congress

Over the last six months, the left flank of the Democratic Party cemented its political power, ousting a number of incumbents, while President Trump maintained his status as the GOP kingmaker — despite suffering a handful of high-profile losses as Republicans have fought to hold their majorities in the House and Senate this fall.

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court issued a historic decision reshaping the landmark Voting Rights Act and setting off a final redistricting scramble.

With just 48 days until Election Day, here are the key surprises from the 2026 primaries.

Democratic socialists and far-left progressives surprised many this cycle when they ousted sitting House members, including Congressional Progressive Caucus lawmakers — showcasing the antiestablishment and anti-incumbent energy that dominated this year.

Democratic socialists Darializa Avila Chevalier and Melat Kiros defeated Reps. Adriano Espaillat (N.Y.) and Diana DeGette (Colo.), respectively, while democratic socialist Claire Valdez won the primary for retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez’s (N.Y.) open seat. Donavan McKinney, who was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), ousted Rep. Shri Thanedar in Michigan.

Democratic socialists also scored notable wins in Democratic primaries for Senate — state Rep. Angie Nixon, a member of the DSA, defeated Trump whistleblower Alex Vindman in a Florida Democratic House primary, while democratic socialist N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas won against the establishment favorite Jim Priest in Oklahoma.

DSA candidates even fared well down the ballot, such as when state Rhode Island state Rep. David Morales defeated incumbent Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary for Providence mayor .

Fetterman makes cameo at GOP midterm convention

One of the most unexpected developments away from the ballot box was Sen. John Fetterman’s (D-Pa.) surprise video appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

Fetterman lauded his Republican colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.), and vowed that the pair would work with Trump to protect the state’s steel industry. Democrats were furious with the move as the senior senator increasingly isolates himself from his party.

“I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid,” Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) told reporters last week. “Those who went out and knocked doors for him — they are absolutely livid.”

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin gubernatorial challenger Francesca Hong were set to dominate their primary races, according to polls ahead of the contest.

Yet, El-Sayed barely defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), while Hong ultimately lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D).

Charles Franklin, director of the Marquette Law School Poll, told The Hill that his polling accurately described the amount of support Hong got in the primary — just shy of 40 percent — while explaining that the fast-moving primary, and the suspension of several campaigns, shifted the dynamics.

“I think the polling also correctly showed that there was a reservoir of undecided voters for someone potentially to capture, and as it turned out, I think that reservoir was reluctant to back Hong,” Franklin said, noting that the Wisconsin race exemplified “a very fluid primary campaign” rather than a “classic polling mess.”

Still, the polling industry as a whole has come under scrutiny this cycle after it was revealed that two polls in the Wisconsin gubernatorial and Los Angeles mayor’s race were completely faked.

The possibility of Trump making an endorsement in the Texas Senate GOP primary runoff kept Republicans on pins and needles this spring.

The Atlantic reported in early March that Trump was expected to endorse Cornyn, and the GOP senator notably finished first in the three-way primary between himself, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas). Yet, Trump’s decision to eventually back Paxton just a week before the May runoff took many by surprise.

“I think it had more to do with Trump ratcheting up another victory on his belt rather than an endorsement of Paxton,” observed Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University.

Veteran Graham Platner sought to capitalize on the antiestablishment sentiment this cycle, pitching his economic populist vision in his quest to take on Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). His candidacy disrupted Maine politics to such an extent that Gov. Janet Mills (D) dropped out of the Democratic primary.

But the surprises didn’t stop there: Two women accused the oyster farmer of sexual misconduct, including sexual assault — causing the progressive’s campaign to implode. He had previously come under fire for controversial Reddit posts.

The stunning rise and eventual fall of Platner’s campaign was particularly notable given Democrats largely lined up behind the candidate as their only hope to oust Collins.

Democrats ultimately nominated former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson as their pick to replace Graham on the ballot, roughly 100 days ahead of Election Day .

The Supreme Court’s decision to dismantle part of the Voting Rights Act this summer paved the way for Republicans in the South to quickly redraw their congressional maps in time for the midterms.

Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama and Florida all changed their maps, but experts only expect a mild net gain for Republicans amid their national redistricting campaign.

“My range is two to six [GOP pickups] right now,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics.

“The map is still, on balance, certainly better for Republicans than it was in 2024, but not so much better … that it makes Republicans” the favorite to hold the majority, he added.

Trump easily exacts vengeance on political foes

Trump toppled a series of Republicans on his blacklist this cycle.

Cornyn, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), all of whom have criticized Trump, lost their primary bids by several points after Trump endorsed their opponents. Cassidy notably voted to convict Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attacks.

Trump also boasted a largely successful track record in House and Senate races, though he suffered blows in a series of high-profile gubernatorial primaries.

“With the erosion of his approval ratings, his ability to push the candidates he supported over the top diminished,” Jones said.

articles.title: Trump’s allies eye big spending cuts as part of postelection agenda
articles.summary: Senate conservatives allied with President Trump are laying the groundwork for substantial cuts to federal spending in the postelection, lame-duck Congress to offset tens of billions of dollars in new defense spending, including funding for the war in Iran, if Democrats pick up seats on Election Day. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) announced Tuesday…
articles.body:
Senate conservatives allied with President Trump are laying the groundwork for substantial cuts to federal spending in the postelection, lame-duck Congress to offset tens of billions of dollars in new defense spending, including funding for the war in Iran, if Democrats pick up seats on Election Day.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) announced Tuesday that the Senate will not consider another budget resolution to unlock the reconciliation process to circumvent a Democratic filibuster until after the Nov. 3 election.

He said he would prefer to pass emergency defense funding to help cover the costs of the Iran war and a boost to the Pentagon’s base budget through the regular appropriations process.

But Thune acknowledged that Republicans will work on a third budget reconciliation package if necessary to get around a potential Democratic filibuster.

Another big priority is the president’s demand to raise the federal debt limit by another $5 trillion or so to extend the nation’s borrowing authority through the end of his term, which expires in January 2029.

Any increase in the debt limit before the end of this year would need to be done through the budget reconciliation process to avoid a Democratic filibuster in the Senate, but getting 51 votes for the proposal in the Senate and 218 votes in the House won’t be an easy task.

Conservative Republicans in both chambers are having discussions about spending reforms they would want in return for any package that increases defense spending and raises the debt limit.

“I’ve had a variety of conversations” about spending offsets to include in a budget reconciliation package, said Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.). “Inflation is a problem. We all understand the cost of living is a problem. The only way we’re going to get the cost of living down is if we balance the budget.”

“Whatever we spend, we’ve got to pay for it,” he added. “If we’re going to talk about debt ceiling, we’re going to have to figure out how we’re going to get spending under control or we’re not going to see lower interest rates, we’re not going to see inflation go away.”

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), who plans to ramp up conversations with colleagues about a third budget reconciliation package, says at least $250 billion in annual wasteful spending could be cut in the lame-duck Congress.

“There will be multiple incentives. Can you thread the needle? It’s a pretty small needle,” Johnson said.

He said Senate and House conservatives have been meeting on a “weekly basis” to lay the groundwork for spending cuts to accompany a multitrillion-dollar increase in the debt limit.

“We’ve basically come to the realization if we want some fiscal controls, that’s the point in time to do it, so we need to be in favor of a debt limit and offer those types of fiscal controls,” he said. “That’s initially what reconciliation was for, deficit reduction.”

Johnson said he will push for between $250 billion and $1 trillion in annual cuts in wasteful spending to offset the costs of big increases in defense spending and other items included in the reconciliation package.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said any budget reconciliation package to pass emergency defense funding and raise the debt limit would need to enact substantial spending reforms to get his vote.

“I wouldn’t vote to raise the debt ceiling unless we significantly reformed how we spend money,” he said. “That would have to include sending it to the Finance Committee, it would have to include instructions to actually reduce spending. There are several Medicaid reforms that could occur, that didn’t occur [last year], that could actually reduce spending.”

It could be Republicans’ last chance to implement spending reforms if Democrats win control of the House in November, an outcome political handicappers project is likely. Democrats have a shot at winning the Senate majority as well, according to nonpartisan analysts.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said Tuesday he expects the Senate will need to pass a third budget reconciliation package to boost defense funding and help cover the costs of the Iran war, which has depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles.

Trump asked Congress in June to provide $67 billion in emergency defense funding, including $21 billion to replenish missile stockpiles.

But defense hawks are pushing for more than $300 billion in defense funding to be included in the budget reconciliation package — a number that Democrats will balk at after Republicans refused to increase nondefense programs by similar percentages.

Thune said Tuesday he’ll punt fights over the budget resolution, emergency defense spending and raising the debt limit until after the election.

“Not before the election, no. That will probably be a postelection question,” he said.

Thune told reporters after the weekly Senate GOP policy luncheon that he would prefer to pass emergency defense spending with Democratic support through the regular appropriations process.

“The defense authorization bill at some point needs to be a bipartisan bill, it just does,” he said. “And I would argue the same thing with respect to appropriations when it comes to national security. The best way to do it is under regular order through the normal appropriations process or perhaps a supplemental.”

Still, Thune said a third budget reconciliation package would be an “option” if Democrats block defense funding.

Republican members of the Senate Appropriations Committee want the Trump administration to make more of an effort to reach out to Senate Democrats to build bipartisan support for emergency defense funding.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) said “Democrats who are interested in the defense of the country need to be educated and brought into the fold” to support increases in defense funding through the regular appropriations process.

“We ought to be addressing funding in a supplemental” spending bill that moves under regular order “as compared to reconciliation,” he said.

“Anything that we can do that puts Republicans and Democrats in the same room with defense experts … is important to lay the groundwork” for spending legislation, he added.

articles.title: Trump seeks to help Republican in uphill North Carolina battle
articles.summary: Republicans are hoping President Trump can give North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley a much-needed boost as Democrats appear increasingly optimistic about flipping the state in November. Trump is slated to travel to the state, the only battleground he has won three times, to stump with Whatley on Wednesday. The visit comes as recent polling…
articles.body:
Republicans are hoping President Trump can give North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley a much-needed boost as Democrats appear increasingly optimistic about flipping the state in November.

Trump is slated to travel to the state, the only battleground he has won three times, to stump with Whatley on Wednesday.

The visit comes as recent polling shows Whatley trailing former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) by double digits in the race.

Forty-nine percent of likely voters said they backed Cooper, while 38 percent said they supported Whatley, according to an Elon University poll released Monday. Another 14 percent said they were undecided or planned to vote for someone else.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the race’s rating from “toss-up” to “lean Democratic” in April.

The campaign stop in the Charlotte suburb of Gastonia is Trump’s first since last week’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where he sought to galvanize the party’s base by urging Republican voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot.

The problem for the GOP is that Trump’s approval rating across the country and in North Carolina has dipped, putting Republicans at risk in the midterms.

Fifty-four percent of North Carolina adults said they disapproved of Trump’s job, while only 31 percent said they approved, according to the same Elon poll.

“It’s 2026. It’s a difficult year if you have an R next to your name wherever you are,” Republican strategist Doug Heye said.

The leading issues in North Carolina match the national ones, starting with affordability and data centers.

Democrats have sought to draw attention to an Associated Press report that a convicted sex offender gave the opening prayer at a Whatley rally earlier this summer. Whatley’s campaign told the outlet it did not plan or organize the event, and Whatley did not know the person.

A Cooper campaign spokesperson linked the timing of the Trump event to the story and said Cooper “is the only candidate with plans to make stuff cost,” while saying Whatley “pushed for policies that spiked his own stocks.”

Whatley faces a uniquely formidable candidate in Cooper, who has won the state four times as governor, including when Trump won it in 2016 and 2020.

Republicans point to Trump’s track record of winning North Carolina three times, including when current Gov. Josh Stein (D) was elected in 2024. They are hoping Trump can help Whatley and GOP candidates up and down the ballot.

“He helps Michael Whatley in trying to energize the Republican base, which is something Republicans have to do,” said Paul Shumaker, a North Carolina-based Republican strategist.

In a statement to The Hill, Whatley’s campaign said he was looking forward to welcoming Trump to the state.

“No one fires up Republicans to get out and vote like President Trump does and his visit is an important part of turning out Republicans to the polls this November,” campaign spokesperson DJ Griffin said.

One Republican operative referenced a High Point University poll showing Cooper’s 8-point lead in April decreasing to 5 points in August among likely voters as evidence that Whatley is gaining ground.

But Cooper as a candidate has been able to defy an energized Republican base in the past.

In 2024, Trump won North Carolina by 3.21 points, while Stein carried the race by just less than 15 points. The president won the state by an even closer margin in 2020, carrying it by just more than 1 point. Cooper, on the other hand, won reelection in 2020 by 4.5 points. Trump carried North Carolina by 3.6 points in 2016, while Cooper unseated then-Gov. Pat McCrory (R) by less than a percentage point.

“Trump won by close margins. I think there’s an attitude in D.C. that because it’s gone red presidential every four years with sort of the blip of Obama, that it’s just an automatic red seat,” Heye said. “It’s just not true.”

Former President Obama flipped the state in 2008 by roughly 7 points before losing it in 2012 by 2 points.

Republicans argue that Whately campaigning with Trump can appeal to persuadable voters if Trump stays laser-focused on affordability.

“He needs to address the affordability issues as it relates to fixing the economy and unaffiliated voters,” Shumaker said. “Unaffiliated voters make up 40 percent of the voting electorate. They will be the single largest block of voters in November.”

“They supported him in the past because of their belief he was going to be front and center in addressing economic concerns, so he needs to start to help addressing economic concerns for Michael Whatley,” he said.

articles.title: Von der Leyen se dirige a los españoles, en especial a los ceutíes: "La frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea. Porque Ceuta es España. Ceuta es Europa"
articles.standfirst: La presidenta de la Unión Europea avisa: “Europa necesita disponer de los medios para proteger sus fronteras en todo momento"
articles.summary: La presidenta de la Unión Europea avisa: “Europa necesita disponer de los medios para proteger sus fronteras en todo momento"
articles.body: La crisis migratoria de Ceuta sigue su camino y la preocupación que ahonda en Europa se ha visto reflejada con las manifestaciones de la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula Von der Leyen. Ha lanzado un mensaje de apoyo al pueblo español y más en concreto a los ceutíes. Lo ha hecho en el debate del Estado de la Unión Europea para pronunciarse al respecto de esta situación. La frase es contundente donde las haya. Muy directa. Dirigida a todos los españoles y en concreto a los de la zona en cuestión. “La frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea. Porque Ceuta es España. Ceuta es Europa. Y Europa estará a vuestro lado”, ha manifestado de forma rotunda. De hecho, ha añadido: “Europa necesita disponer de los medios para proteger sus fronteras en todo momento, sobre todo ante escenarios en los que se provocan y utilizan como arma movimientos masivos de personas”. El pleno del Parlamento Europeo reunido en Estrasburgo ha planteado la creación de un instrumento de respuesta europeo para hacer frente a entradas masivas de irregulares. Por ello, ha insistido en la necesidad de que los 27 países miembro apliquen el Pacto de Migración que endurece la frontera exterior y agiliza las deportaciones, al tiempo que ha apuntado nuevas medidas para tratar que la Unión reaccione con urgencia ante eventuales crisis futuras similares a la de Ceuta, si bien la conservadora alemana ha evitado toda referencia al papel de Marruecos en la entrada irregular de casi 80.000 personas a finales de julio. La presidenta ha puntualizado que se ha registrado una reducción del 55 % en las llegadas irregulares en los últimos dos años y un descenso adicional del 35 % este año. “Se trata de un avance real”, ha recalcado la presidenta de la Comisión Europea.

articles.title: Trump’s $5,000 handout is an insult to conservatism
articles.summary: Sounds to me like using federal tax dollars to buy votes.
articles.body:
President Trump gathered his hardcore MAGA faithful in Dallas last week at the Republican National Convention to officially energize his base to vote in the upcoming midterm election. In reality, the gathering was about paying homage again and again to Trump’s outsized ego.

The lesson from Dallas is that if calling the other guy a “communist” is the best you can do, you have a serious problem. That applies especially if your own administration is implicitly adopting a leading tenet of socialism — government ownership of the means of production — by taking a federal government stake in 30 private sector companies.

Another nod to socialism came during Trump’s closing remarks on the second night of the convention, when he promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult citizen if the Republicans keep control of both the House and the Senate. Sounds to me like using federal tax dollars to buy votes.

Someone in the White House needs to realize as soon as possible that the Republicans’ 2026 electoral problem is not a lack of government handouts.

As Trump pushes the federal government into seemingly every aspect of American life, some of us long for the keystone of conservative philosophy as President Ronald Reagan enunciated : “Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.”

The Wall Street Journal’s Kimberly Strassel recently spelled out the Republicans’ midterm turnout problem with research showing a lack of enthusiasm by Republicans who do not consider themselves part of Trump’s MAGA movement. That makes perfect sense when you understand that Trump’s entire second term has been all about governing for his own diehards.

Trump’s insistence on making this election about himself and a referendum on his second term is exactly the wrong strategy. His approval rating in a consortium of respected polls is 40 percent because he has spent the last 20 months catering to MAGA and MAGA only. In the process, he has driven away thoughtful voters who want the government to deal with significant problems like grocery prices while working competently on issues that need attention without using egocentric ultimatums and overkill.

Let’s be clear. The MAGA base alone will not win an election for anyone, including Trump and Vice President JD Vance. It is precisely what it is called: a base, meaning it must be built from. Elections are won by addition and inclusion. Trump’s understanding of how to build from that base is apparently nonexistent.

Perhaps Trump could get away with his $5,000 offer because his largesse with other people’s money included all adults. Fellow conservatives who may first find the idea interesting should consider this:

Will you be happy when the guy passing out Democratic Socialist of America flyers down the street gets his $5,000 check? Will you be happy when every single person working in the congressional office of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) each gets their $5,000? And will you be absolutely thrilled when you discover that the performers in the local drag queen show spent the afternoon discussing what outfits to spend their $5,000 in taxpayer money on?

As per usual with Trump, his pronouncement lacks specificity. Would the giveaway be means-tested or even perhaps tested by length of citizenship?

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), a true conservative, rightly dismissed the proposal, saying it “will lead to more debt and more inflation.” Conservative Republican Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) said: “Some of us think dependency is evil and soul sucking in all its forms.”

Then there is the fiscal aspect. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget called the president’s political gimmick “fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious.” It estimates the cost at $1.2 trillion dollars . We have not yet heard from Trump’s Office of Management and Budget on the proposal, but one wonders if they knew anything about it in advance.

Trump’s second term presidency has operated on the governing principle that if it comes into his head, it comes out of his mouth. At the same time, it seems that Trump’s gut has lost touch with hard-working American families. That is a problem for which there is no cure before Nov. 3.

Kevin Igoe is the former deputy chief of staff of the Republican National Committee and former executive director of the Maryland Republican Party. He served as chief of staff of the Maryland Department of Budget and Management and was a Reagan White House appointee.

articles.summary: A major abortion rights group is expanding its outreach efforts in key battleground House districts ahead of November’s midterm elections. Reproductive Freedom for All (RFFA) said it is investing about $1 million into a direct voter contact campaign across three priority districts in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada. According to details shared first with The Hill,…
articles.body:
A major abortion rights group is expanding its outreach efforts in key battleground House districts ahead of November’s midterm elections .

Reproductive Freedom for All (RFFA) said it is investing about $1 million into a direct voter contact campaign across three priority districts in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada.

According to details shared first with The Hill, the effort will support paid canvassing and voter engagement in: Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, where Democrat Amish Shah is running to unseat Rep. Dave Schweikert (R); Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, where Democrat Christina Hines is looking to capture the open seat currently held by Rep. John James (R), who is running for governor; and Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, where incumbent Rep. Susie Lee (D) is trying to fend off GOP challenger Marty O’Donnell.

The effort is part of the organization’s overall $23.5 million midterm investment to mobilize voters and flip contested GOP-held districts blue.

Voter anger about abortion rights after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 helped propel Democrats to a series of midterm victories that year.

Abortion isn’t the top-tier national issue for Democrats this cycle, though the fight has continued in many states.

RFFA is trying to keep abortion front and center, especially in states that will be voting on abortion-related ballot measures.

For instance, the canvassing effort will also work to turn out support for Question 6 in Nevada, which voters must approve for a second time in 2026 for abortion rights protections to be added to the state’s constitution.

“Control of Congress — and our ability to fight back against national attacks on reproductive freedom — could come down to these races with razor-thin margins,” RFFA President and CEO Mini Timmaraju said in a statement.

With affordability as a top concern among the electorate this year, Timmaraju noted her organization has been working to frame abortion as an economic issue that all voters should care about.

“This investment will power meaningful conversations with voters about what is at stake and why electing champions of reproductive freedom is crucial this November,” she said.

articles.title: On the Hill, Democrats are creating a weapon that might backfire on them
articles.summary: The problem was never oversight. It’s oversight that only ever points in one partisan direction.
articles.body:
CNN reported this week that House Democrats are building a new legal weapon for 2027: civil lawsuits forcing compliance with congressional subpoenas. This is the latest instrument in what conservatives call “lawfare.”

It is aimed at the Iran war, the White House ballroom project, the Trump family’s business dealings, and the Epstein files.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who could chair the House Judiciary Committee next year, says that a majority would give Democrats “a lot more authority to get ourselves into court.” That’s fair enough. But before anyone sharpens this new blade, it is worth checking whose fingerprints are on the handle.

Right now, as a minority in Congress, House Democrats can send letters and hold press conferences. They cannot force anyone to answer.

If they win the majority, they will gain committee gavels, subpoena power, contempt votes, and, as Raskin referenced, one new option: asking federal judges to order compliance instead of waiting on Trump’s own Justice Department to prosecute him.

This innovation will probably be slower than advertised. The fight over former White House Counsel Don McGahn’s testimony, for example, ran from 2019 to 2021 and ended in a negotiated deal, not a courtroom victory. Subpoena litigation measures progress in years, not in news cycles.

Then there’s the target list. Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), likely the next Armed Services Committee chairman , won’t rule out subpoenas for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran and a string of firings. None of that proves wrongdoing — a subpoena is a question, not a verdict. But Pentagon privilege and classification fights alone can eat a congressional term.

State attorneys general, meanwhile, filed at least 156 multistate lawsuits against Trump’s first term. NYU’s Institute for Policy Integrity found that the administration lost the large majority of agency-action cases. Litigation isn’t a boutique tool anymore — it’s standard equipment.

The Senate Judiciary Committee spent 2026 unwinding Arctic Frost, the Biden-era FBI probe behind Special Counsel Jack Smith’s case against Trump. Grassley’s committee has made public 197 grand jury subpoenas covering more than 430 Republican individuals and organizations. He confirmed that phone carriers turned over phone records tied to eight Republican senators and now-FBI Director Kash Patel . If pulling senators’ phone records counts as “oversight,” then so does subpoenaing a defense secretary’s calendar.

Congress doesn’t get to define ‘legitimate legislative purpose’ as ‘whatever my party happens to be doing this year’ — not this Congress, not the next one, no matter who holds the gavel.”

The election interference case in Georgia added another wrinkle: The Biden White House Counsel’s Office told Fulton County prosecutors in September 2022 that it would not assert executive privilege over former Trump officials’ testimony. That cleared a path for Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis’s case. That alone shows it was never quite true that Biden’s White House stayed out of the case.

The Epstein files cut the other way. Former Vice President Kamala Harris later said the Biden administration kept “an absolute separation” from the Justice Department’s Epstein file for four years rather than push for release. Nobody discovered a taste for transparency until the files became useful as a weapon against Trump.

The same was true of classified documents. The Justice Department that raided Mar-a-Lago in August 2022 answered to a president who was storing his own classified material next to a Corvette in his Wilmington garage . Special Counsel Robert Hur documented this and still declined to recommend charges . Both men mishandled classified records, but only one got the search warrant.

To be sure, oversight is a real constitutional function, not a dirty word. Congress has every right to know whether taxpayer money built a ballroom or whether Pentagon officials misled lawmakers about war powers. Raskin has a point that courts beat negotiation for prying documents loose. Real oversight protects people who have no other way to get a straight answer.

The problem was never oversight. It’s oversight that only ever points in one partisan direction.

So here is a modest proposal for whoever runs the House come January: Pass a standing rule, not a press release, spelling out what makes a subpoena legitimate and which privileges apply, binding both parties equally. Do that, and Democrats get their day in court on the ballroom. Republicans get theirs on Arctic Frost. Nobody gets to invent the rules mid-game just because they hold the gavel.

Failing that, Trump has a simpler option, and former President Joe Biden already wrote the template when he pardoned members of his own family on his way out the door in January 2025. If Trump wants to take the wind out of the coming subpoena fleet before it leaves the dock, the precedent is signed, sealed, and sitting in the Federal Register.

Louis Brandeis said sunlight is the best disinfectant. He never said it only shines on one party’s porch.

Before Congress builds a permanent legal weapon for whoever wins in November, it should build permanent rules for using it, because in Washington, the next subpoena fight is never really the last one.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: Supreme Court’s mail ballot ruling brings giant sigh of relief to Trump critics
articles.summary: Nevada’s top election official was at dinner with a friend on Monday night when his phone started blowing up. The Supreme Court’s mail ballot decision had landed. His stomach sank. “Then, as I started to read, just pure emotion of joy,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar (D) told The Gavel. While Trump expressed dismay, the…
articles.body:
Nevada’s top election official was at dinner with a friend on Monday night when his phone started blowing up. The Supreme Court’s mail ballot decision had landed. His stomach sank.

“Then, as I started to read, just pure emotion of joy,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar (D) told The Gavel.

While Trump expressed dismay, the Supreme Court’s decision to keep a block on his mail-in voting plan is being met with relief from the president’s critics, who had warned that chaos would ensue if the plan were allowed.

It would’ve required states to meet new ballot design requirements and upload lists of voters for them to receive a mail ballot.

But some states had already begun sending ballots.

Aguilar, who also serves as chair of the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State, worked through the weekend to develop a Plan B as the justices’ decision loomed. He was even considering launching a new lawsuit against the U.S. Postal Service under state law.

“What are some of the crazy ideas? Let’s throw ideas on the board. Let’s figure it out so that we can then be ready to go,” Aguilar recounted.

That is no longer needed. With Trump’s plan on hold, Nevada and other states are proceeding with mail-in voting as they have previously.

It was a rare loss for Trump on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket. But Aguilar said he was optimistic after listening earlier this year to questioning from Justice Amy Coney Barrett and Chief Justice John Roberts during oral arguments in another case, Watson v. Republican National Committee . The two conservatives later joined the liberal justices to side against the GOP in that case and rule that officials can accept mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.

Both Barrett and Roberts appeared to rule against the president again in the latest dispute, though the justices don’t have to disclose their votes in emergency rulings.

“I would assume that they understood the situation pretty well, especially being so close to the election and what disruption and chaos that would cause,” Aguilar said.

NAACP General Counsel Kristen Clarke told The Gavel that Trump’s plan would have been “simply catastrophic.”

“There is no way that the midterm election cycle would have been a normal one had the Supreme Court given the administration the green light to turn our mail voting system on its head,” said Clarke.

Monday’s ruling saw him heap some of his most searing condemnation to date on Barrett and his two other Supreme Court nominees, Justice Neil Gorsuch and Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The post showed how Trump’s limited series of Supreme Court losses still looms large in the president’s social media feed. He went on to condemn the justices’ recent decisions striking down his tariffs and birthright citizenship restrictions.

“It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court,” Trump concluded.

Like Barrett, Gorsuch didn’t explain himself. Kavanaugh did. He penned a solo opinion suggesting that Trump’s efforts may be legal, but it’s simply too close to the midterms to implement them.

So, what does the Supreme Court’s ruling mean? Trump’s plan is effectively dead for 2026 but remains an open question for the 2028 cycle.

It all depends how you interpret the ruling’s key sentence:

“The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction.”

That may not seem like much at a glance, but there’s a lot to unpack. Irv Gornstein , executive director of Georgetown Law’s Supreme Court Institute, during a discussion with reporters on Tuesday, called the language “cryptic.”

The justices could’ve written something like: The U.S. Postal Service’s plan is likely unlawful.

Instead, they zeroed in on the judge’s preliminary ruling. That ruling concerns only the midterms and leaves future election cycles unaddressed.

So, were the justices trying to leave the door open, or were they suggesting that Trump’s policy actually exceeds his power, no matter the timing?

Gornstein suggested it may be the latter. After all, Kavanaugh felt a need to speak out separately from the majority to indicate Trump may be acting legally once the calendar isn’t a problem. No other justice was willing to join him, at least publicly.

It “suggests to me that one or two justices were fine with sending a subtle signal that they would rather not see this again but were not fine with sending a definitive signal that they did not want to see this again,” Gornstein said.

“We will see whether the Trump administration takes the subtle hint.”

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

NY, others sue over public charge rule: New York is leading a coalition of 22 states and Washington, D.C., in challenging a Trump administration rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards if they rely on public benefits such as food stamps. Blue cities filed a separate suit .

FEMA cuts ruled unlawful : A federal judge in California says the Department of Homeland Security “ unlawfully usurped the authority ” of the Federal Emergency Management Agency when it tried to cut the workforce in half, ruling the proposal unlawful .

ICE at polling sites?: The city of Denver is suing the Trump administration to block the presence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers at polling locations for the midterms. Border czar Tom Homan says there is “no plan” to put them there.

Trump-era visa policy halted: A judge blocked a Trump administration policy that would’ve restricted how long foreign students and journalists on visas can remain in the country.

Trump’s name on Kennedy Center, blocked: A judge ruled the latest attempt to add Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center’s exterior is unlawful. The ruling also blocks plans to name the performing arts institution’s outdoor plaza after the president.

Kavanaugh recounts being at White House on 9/11: Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was at the White House working for then-President George W. Bush during the Sept. 11 attacks, recounted his experiences at a Notre Dame panel on Friday’s anniversary. “Seared into my memory is the Secret Service agent saying, ‘Run! Sprint! Ladies take off your heels, and sprint!’ And we were all kind of sprinting out the gate,” Kavanaugh told the crowd.

It’s been a busy summer for courts in the nation’s capital.

That was evident Tuesday morning, when a steady stream of lawyers, defendants and onlookers flowed into the D.C. Superior Court courtroom where Associate Judge Deborah Israel was presiding over more than a dozen criminal case hearings.

The local trial court calendar was so full that the judge informed everyone the proceedings were delayed because she was waiting for attorneys to check in.

One attorney even told a client that he was needed in three different courtrooms that morning but promised to be back in time for the appearance.

We were there for a status conference involving Zion Mitchell , a 21-year-old National Guard member accused of pointing a gun at a fellow guardsman during an argument late last month.

Here’s what happened, according to prosecutors:

Mitchell and a group of National Guard members were on break from patrol duty on Aug. 25, sitting in a black van in front of a Popeyes fast food restaurant on H Street NE. He was roughly two months into his deployment.

He and the alleged victim, identified in court only as N.J. , got into a heated exchange over whether their hairstyles complied with Army regulations. Mitchell threatened to “slap the Jackson 5” out of her and a back-and-forth ensued, with the victim ultimately saying: “Shut the f— up. Try me.”

The alleged victim then heard a “holster click,” later finding out Mitchell had drawn his weapon. One witness allegedly told him to “Put that up.” Another described the gun as being loaded — as National Guard firearms typically are — with one round in the chamber.

Mitchell initially told authorities that he was in a “playful argument” with the victim, suggesting that his pulling out a magazine and pistol was part of “playful banter.” But he later admitted that he pointed the gun in her direction, at a roughly 45-degree angle and not toward her head.

The National Guardsman was arrested in early September and charged with assault with a dangerous weapon and possession of a firearm while committing a crime of violence or dangerous crime. Assistant U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jasmine Dohemann told the judge a potential plea offer was on the table.

Mitchell, who lives in Georgia, was brought into the courtroom wearing an orange jumpsuit and in shackles. He had been in jail since his arrest, with a magistrate judge initially denying bond due to the “nature of the crimes.”

Israel released Mitchell on bond, noting that hadn’t engaged in “smart behavior” but also had no prior interaction with the judicial system. His record was “as clean as it gets,” she said.

But she added a few conditions. He was to be fitted with a GPS tracker and ordered to live with his mother in Stone Mountain, Ga. He cannot leave the greater Atlanta area, is under a 6 p.m.-to-6 a.m. curfew, cannot possess any firearms and is barred from contacting the victim.

If the National Guard tried to deploy him elsewhere, the judge told Mitchell’s attorney that she needed to be notified.

Just down the road in the E. Barrett Prettyman U.S. Courthouse, where federal cases are heard, another set of high-profile proceedings was unfolding.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper had called a scheduling conference in an ongoing legal challenge to the Kennedy Center’s plan to add Trump’s name to the building. He had already blocked the move once, finding that it was unlikely unlawful because Congress hadn’t approved.

A couple of hours later, the Obama appointee would issue another injunction that temporarily stops the board from adding the lettering back to the facade — this time in the form of two inscriptions that seek to recognize the president’s fundraising efforts.

The Justice Department, which is representing the Kennedy Center, is expected to appeal.

In another part of the courthouse, a jury was beginning to hear evidence in the federal trial of a D.C. councilmember charged with bribery.

Trayon White Sr. , the councilmember for Ward 8, stands accused of accepting more than $150,000 in exchange for using his position on the council to “pressure government employees” into extending contracts for two companies that provide violence intervention services. He has pleaded not guilty.

White was captured on video collecting $35,000 in cash on four separate occasions in the summer of 2024. That fact, the jury heard, was undisputed.

The councilman, who won a special election in July 2025 to retake his vacant seat, appeared in the courtroom in a beige jacket and waistcoat. He seemed relaxed but engaged, occasionally chatting with his counsel as the first witness was on the stand.

During a 10-minutes recess following opening arguments, White moved freely about the room, hugging some who had come to watch. Several people lined the hall outside, waiting patiently for a seat in the packed gallery to open.

White faces up to 15 years in prison and the loss of his seat, if convicted.

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases that we are keeping an eye on…

The Supreme Court’s new term is nearly here. The justices kick things off with their first closed-door conference on Sept. 28, when they will vote on new cases to take up.

That initial meeting is a big one. The justices will confront nearly 900 petitions to accept cases that have piled up over the summer. Court watchers nickname it the “long conference.”

We’ve gone through the petition list. Over the next three editions of The Gavel, we’ll preview cases that could pique the justices’ interest along with other interesting ones.

This week, we’ll focus on the requests from state attorneys general and challenges to state laws:

Maryland gun law: Gun owners and Second Amendment groups are challenging Maryland gun regulations that prohibit possessing a firearm in various public areas. It’s the latest case to test the bounds of “sensitive places” where the government can ban firearms. The challengers say the restrictions don’t survive the Supreme Court’s recent Second Amendment cases. The case is Novotny v. Moore .

Iowa immigration law: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird (R) wants to enforce the state’s law that makes it a crime to illegally re-enter without proper legal status. Lower courts ruled it was preempted by federal law and blocked the statute before it went into effect. The state argues the challengers had no standing to do so and that decision was wrong on the merits. The case is Bird v. Iowa Migrants Movement for Justice .

Juvenile murder conviction in Utah: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown’s (R) office is appealing a decision from its state supreme court wiping the sentence of Morris Mullins, then 17, who was convicted of aggravated murder for killing a 78-year-old woman. Utah wants the justices to decide if it’s constitutional to sentence a juvenile murderer to life without parole when a court finds they are capable of change. The case is Utah v. Mullins .

Post-conviction relief in Arkansas: Under a 1996 law that is aimed at stopping prisoners from endless legal maneuvers to fight their convictions, state inmates have a one-year statute of limitation to file a habeas petition. That clock pauses when the person has a “properly filed” pending application for post-conviction relief. In this case, the defendant was asking the Arkansas courts for permission to file a belated appeal. The lower court ruled that it counted, and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin (R) wants the high court to take a look. The case is Payne v. Garrett .

Other miscellaneous, notable petitions in the pipeline:

Municipal liability: Both sides in this dispute want the Supreme Court to take up their case, but for different reasons. Richard Hershey filed the lawsuit after Bossier City, La., police threatened him with arrest for handing out pamphlets promoting the Christian Vegetarian Association on a sidewalk. Hershey wants the Supreme Court to review whether the lower court properly granted the officers qualified immunity. The city wants the justices to consider whether their precedents allow the city to be held liable for constitutional violations for a single incident. Each side is represented by well-known conservative Supreme Court advocates. The cases are Bossier City, La. v. Hershey and Hershey v. Bossier City, La.

Military divorce: Roxane and Richard Marschner’s divorce settlement said Richard would make it up to his ex-wife if her share of his military retirement pay was reduced because he later waived it to receive disability benefits. However, North Dakota’s top court held that agreement is preempted by the federal Uniformed Services Former Spouses’ Protection Act under the logic of a 2017 Supreme Court decision. Roxane appealed. The case is Marschner v. Marschner .

‘Let’s Go Brandon’ shirt: Two brothers who were punished by a Michigan school district for wearing sweatshirts to class that read “Let’s Go Brandon,” a phrase used to mock former President Biden, are appealing after a lower court sided with the district. Their petition invokes the Supreme Court’s 1969 landmark decision protecting students who wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. The new case is D.A. v. Tri County Area Schools .

The 1 st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear arguments in the Trump administration’s bid to dismantle the Minority Business Development Agency, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and other agencies. A judge declared it unlawful.

The 8 th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear arguments in Missouri’s bid to use a GOP-friendly congressional map for the midterms. The Supreme Court has blocked the map as the case proceeds.

The Judicial Conference — the federal judiciary’s policymaking arm — will hold its biannual meeting.

Barrett is slated to give a book talk at the UVA Karsh Institute of Democracy in Charlottesville, Va.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson is set to receive the Justice Brennan Distinguished Jurist Award at the Philadelphia Bar Association’s annual conference.

Anthony Kazmierczak will be sentenced after pleading guilty to an assault charge for spraying Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) with apple cider vinegar during a January town hall.

Melissa Farris , accused of defacing the World War II Memorial on the National Mall, will be arraigned in D.C. Superior Court on felony vandalism charges

The University of Chicago will host its annual Supreme Court preview event.

A federal judge in Boston will hold a hearing on the legality of the Trump-era reversal of a longstanding policy to not conduct immigration enforcement at “sensitive locations,” like houses of worship. The policy is currently blocked under an existing order.

articles.title: Federal judges are being targeted with pizza doxxing; no one has been held to account
articles.summary: A new study revealed that federal judges have faced nearly 200 anonymous pizza deliveries since 2025 as part of a coordinated effort to threaten them, highlighting a lack of resources within the Marshals Service to prosecute those involved.
articles.body:
A Domino’s pizza shows up at a federal judge’s door in the middle of the night. No one in the house ordered it. The message: Someone knows where you live and where your children sleep.

A new study from the Berkeley Judicial Institute and the Rule of Law Lab at NYU School of Law reports nearly 200 anonymous pizza deliveries to federal judges since 2025, targeting judges appointed by presidents of both parties.

At least 20 such deliveries were made in the name of Daniel Anderl — the son of U.S. District Judge Esther Salas. He was killed in 2020 by a disgruntled lawyer who had appeared before Judge Salas. Salas, one of 34 sitting judges with whom we spoke, called the deliveries “a veiled threat, warning the judge that they could end up like me or my son.”

Federal criminal law prohibits such threats , but Salas noted that the people responsible “remain at large.” We found no public record of arrests or prosecutions.

In most cases, the targeted judge had recently ruled against the Trump administration. U.S. District Judge John McConnell was the first to tell Salas he had received a pizza in her son’s name after such a ruling. In March 2025, Justice Amy Coney Barrett received one after joining an opinion the administration opposed; family members in South Carolina were targeted around the same time.

Other judges have been targeted simply for speaking out about attacks on colleagues. U.S. District Judge Robert Lasnik and his two adult children, living in different cities, each had pizzas delivered in Daniel Anderl’s name after his criticism of judicial attacks aired on television. Another judge told us that after he spoke on a panel about attacks on the judiciary, he and his panelists — scattered across several states — received pizzas that same evening.

Targeted judges told us that the pizza deliveries are being coordinated across the country, and that the Marshals Service, the agency charged with protecting them, is not equipped to investigate such threats. “With all the pizza deliveries that are occurring all over the country,” remarked a judge, “how is it that we don’t have an answer to date about who is behind these threats?”

Pizza deliveries are just one of many threats facing little accountability. And one has to wonder why. These are orders placed through commercial outlets, with records and delivery logs, used to threaten judges across multiple states. Yet after 200 incidents, no one has been identified.

Several judges, appointed by presidents of both political parties, told us they knew of no arrests or prosecutions relating to the threats they’d faced, even though such threats are clearly prohibited by federal criminal law. Among them was Judge McConnell, who also received at least six credible death threats and whose daughter had her personal information posted online.

U.S. District Judge John Coughenour was “swatted.” Police appeared at his home, guns drawn, after a false report was made that he had just murdered his wife. That gap raises a broader question: Are threats against federal judges being sufficiently investigated and, where appropriate, prosecuted?

The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, the administrative arm of the federal judiciary, has informed Congress that “[s]ecurity incidents of significant concern” increased for judges by 57 percent in fiscal 2025 and are “on pace to rise again” this year. But judges say the Marshals Service, while dedicated, is underfunded and understaffed. The chair of the Judicial Conference’s Committee on Judicial Security, Judge Richard Sullivan, told us it has fewer than 3,900 deputies responsible for protecting roughly 2,500 to 2,700 federal judges nationwide. Its own director has asked Congress for a thousand more deputies. Congress has not funded them.

Federal judges have stayed true to their oath to the Constitution. “We’re all still doing our jobs, without fear or favor,” one judge said. But the personal toll is real and underreported. One judge described spending 45 minutes weighing whether to abandon a ruling he knew was legally sound, just to protect his family. He didn’t, but he said he was “traumatized.” A judge with nearly two decades on the bench, previously unafraid, now instinctively wonders, “Is this the day I’m going to get shot at? … I do feel like we are sitting ducks.”

Judges now avoid answering their doors for unexpected deliveries and have removed office numbers from court websites — making them harder to reach, even for unrepresented litigants. Several worry it will drive judges to leave and deter talented lawyers from joining the bench.

The persistence of coordinated attacks on the judiciary without visible consequence for perpetrators poses a grave threat to our constitutional order. Congress should fund the Marshals Service sufficiently to protect the judges who depend on it, and the Department of Justice should prioritize investigating threats against federal judges. These threats deserve real investigation and prosecution where warranted.

Jeremy Fogel is a retired U.S. District Court Judge and the executive director of the Berkeley Judicial Institute. Amrit Singh is professor of practice and faculty director of the Rule of Law Lab at New York University School of Law.

articles.title: TV news helicopter crashes near deadly L.A. bus collision, 3 killed
articles.summary: Multiple helicopters were over the scene of a bus crash nearby when the chopper descended.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES ( KTLA ) — A local helicopter news reporter and pilot who died in a tragic crash while covering a fatal L.A. Metro bus collision Tuesday in Chatsworth have been identified.

NBC4 and Telemundo reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were over the scene, in which the driver of an SUV slammed into an L.A. Metro bus , killing three people and hospitalizing six others, when their helicopter crashed.

The bus collision occurred at about 5 p.m. at the intersection of West Nordhoff Street and De Soto Avenue, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department. Dozens of firefighters and law enforcement personnel responded to the scene.

LAFD officials said the helicopter went down just before 7 p.m. between two commercial buildings at 9151 N. Mason Ave., with the explosion causing several nearby vehicles and storage containers to erupt in flames.

Firefighters initiated an offensive attack on the blaze and were able to extinguish the flames, while paramedics began pulling victims out of the aircraft for medical triage, fire officials said.

Moreno and Marciniw were killed in the crash, along with another unidentified victim. A lone survivor was rushed to the hospital in unknown condition. Preliminary, though unconfirmed reports, one of the deceased was not on the aircraft but in the area of the crash.

According to Sky5 reporter Gil Leyvas, multiple police and news helicopters, including KTLA’s Sky5, were over the scene of the bus collision at the time the chopper went down.

Aerial footage from the bus crash captured people suddenly running from the scene, along with police cruisers and firefighters speeding toward a fiery explosion just blocks away.

In the moments after the helicopter crash, it was not immediately clear whether the aircraft was a news or police chopper, though multiple local news sources, including the Los Angeles Times , reported that NBC4 had lost contact with its helicopter crew.

Just after 9 p.m., NBC4 confirmed on air that it was the station’s NewsChopper4 that crashed.

Both Southern California natives, Moreno and Marciniw began flying together in 2023, according to NBC Los Angeles.

In a statement posted on its website, NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said :

“We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”

Moreno and Marciniw were both employees of Angel City Air, the same company that owns and operates KTLA’s Sky5.

In response to the dual tragedies, which occurred less than a quarter-mile apart, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass said, “I’m absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash.”

California Gov. Gavin Newsom also weighed in, saying, “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family.”

Officials with the National Transportation Safety Board are leading the investigation into the crash.

“An NTSB investigator is expected to arrive on scene tomorrow morning,” the federal agency said in a statement to KTLA. “We continue to gather information at this time.”
