articles.title: US set to approve 60,000 heavy bombs for Israel: What that means
articles.summary: The package of 2,000-pound bombs comes amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and its occupation of southern Lebanon.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing to sell 60,000 highly destructive, 2,000-pound (907kg) bombs to Israel in a multibillion-dollar package which will be funded by American taxpayers.

US media has reported that the Trump administration has approved the sale, which features some of the most destructive munitions in Western arsenals, and has informally notified Congress.

This is one of the biggest US munition packages to Israel and comes after nearly three years of genocidal war on Gaza, ongoing pogroms by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank and a mighty assault on southern Lebanon – which together have killed tens of thousands and displaced millions in the region.

It also comes as the US’s own munitions stockpile has been depleted due to its war on Iran, with the crisis worsened by Russia’s war on Ukraine.

So, what bombs are the US sending to Israel, and what can Israel do with them?

What weapons are the US planning to sell to Israel?

The Trump administration has not officially confirmed this sale yet. A senior administration official told AFP news agency that “all foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process”, but refused to comment on pending transactions.

Meanwhile, a State Department spokesperson told AFP that “as a matter of policy, the Department does not confirm or comment on proposed arms sales until they have been formally notified to Congress”.

However, Washington is reported to be on track to deliver a munitions package to Israel that is believed to include 60,000 warheads, including 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator.

The sale is worth $2.8bn, the majority of which will be paid for by the US’s Foreign Military Financing scheme, wherein Washington pays Israel from its own taxpayers’ funds to buy American-made weapons and military equipment.

MK-84: The largest among the Mark 80 series of bombs, this unguided, 2,000-pound (907kg) general-purpose bomb is designed primarily for maximum blast and fragmentation against buildings and moderately protected targets. It can destroy buildings and kill or injure people hundreds of metres from the bomb site.

BLU-117: A 2,000-pound (907kg) general-purpose bomb which looks very similar to the MK-84 but has a different explosive filler and can also be fitted with precision-guidance kits. It also has a thermal protective coating, designed for safer storage, particularly by the US Navy.

I-2000 Penetrator: Also referred to as a “bunker buster”, this roughly 2,000-pound-class, hard-target penetrator is designed to punch through hardened structures before detonating; its casing is substantially thicker and harder than an MK-84.

In 2024, then-President Joe Biden’s administration paused the delivery of some 2,000-pound-class bombs to Israel amid growing international criticism by rights groups about the disproportionate number of civilians being killed in attacks.

Trump ended the pause when he returned to the presidency the following year – and bypassed a usual congressional review process to approve a nearly $3bn arms sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of these powerful bombs. In January this year, Washington approved a further package of arms sales to Israel worth $6.67bn.

When has Israel used 2,000-pound US bombs before?

Israel had been using 2,000-pound-class bombs, especially in the occupied Palestinian territory and in Lebanon, for at least four decades prior to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered Israel’s war on Gaza.

In 1981, Israel used this bomb during the Osirak bombing, known as Operation Opera, in an air strike which destroyed an unfinished Iraqi nuclear reactor near Baghdad. The next year, Israel dropped these bombs in Lebanon and Syria, accounting for a high civilian toll during attacks.

According to the Project on Defense Alternatives (PDA), which conducts defence policy research and analysis, a 2,000-pound blast will severely damage, injure or kill everything or anyone within 35 metres (115 feet).

Averaged across different types of surfaces, a 2000-pound bomb will carve out a crater 50 feet (15 metres) across and 16 feet (5 metres) deep.

Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, preliminary research suggests that Israel has used these powerful and destructive bombs more frequently.

For instance, on October 31, 2023, Israel dropped a 2,000-pound bomb on the Jabalia refugee camp in a densely populated area of Gaza City, leaving a giant crater amid bombed-out buildings, and killing dozens of civilians. The UN human rights office said the Israeli air attack could amount to a war crime .

The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in November 2024. Washington has ridiculed the court’s jurisdiction.

According to an Al Jazeera investigation, The Rest of the Story , civil defence teams in Gaza have documented 2,842 Palestinians who witnesses say in effect “evaporated” in the blast of bombs since the war began in October 2023, leaving behind no remains other than blood spray or small fragments of flesh.

Experts and witnesses have attributed this phenomenon to Israel’s systematic use of internationally prohibited thermal and thermobaric weapons, often referred to as vacuum or aerosol bombs, capable of generating temperatures exceeding 3,500 degrees Celsius (6,332 degrees Fahrenheit).

The investigation detailed how specific chemical compositions in Israeli munitions turn human bodies into ash in seconds – and identified specific US-manufactured munitions used in Gaza that are linked to these disappearances, including MK-84 and BLU series bunker busters.

Vasily Fatigarov, a Russian military expert, explained that these weapons do not just kill; they obliterate matter. Unlike conventional explosives, these weapons disperse a cloud of fuel that ignites to create an enormous fireball and a vacuum effect.

“To prolong the burning time, powders of aluminium, magnesium and titanium are added to the chemical mixture,” Fatigarov said. “This raises the temperature of the explosion to between 2,500 and 3,000 degrees Celsius [4,532F to 5,432F].”

Very. Together, 60,000 2,000-pound-class bombs weigh 54,400 tonnes.

That is about the weight of the entire steel skeleton of New York’s Empire State Building. Or seven times the weight of the iron structure of the Eiffel Tower.

Its mass also far exceeds the most infamous single conventional air raid of the 20th century. The March 1945 Tokyo firebombing, which killed more than 80,000 people in one night, used roughly 1,600 tonnes of bombs.

On a broader scale, 54,400 tonnes is nearly the total weight of bombs dropped on Berlin throughout World War II, and also roughly one-third of all bombs that fell on Japan’s home islands.

Isn’t the US running short on munition stockpiles?

Yes, a Pentagon watchdog report released on Monday confirmed earlier media reports that the war on Iran is burning through Washington’s munitions – especially the costly Patriot surface-to-air missile defence system – and creating “bottlenecks” in supply chains.

“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”

President Trump wrote on Truth Social that the US is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.”

What reactions have there been to this weapons sale?

News of the sale has been condemned by figures on both sides of the political spectrum in the US.

“By any definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide,” conservative commentator Tucker Carlson, who has been highly critical of the US support for Israel’s war on Palestine, wrote on X.

“The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region. If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.”

US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat, said he would work to block the sale, and accused the Trump administration of “sending bombs paid for by American taxpayers to a government led by a wanted war criminal”.

Former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, who was affiliated with the Republican Party when in the House of Representatives, wrote: “We did not vote for this. America does not support this. Our tax dollars and weapons have been used to kill tens of thousands of innocent people.”

The US-Israel war on Iran, which started in late February with the assassination of then Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, is widely unpopular in the US, with President Trump’s approval ratings dipping.

A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 percent of voters and 66 percent of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 percent and 20 percent when the question was first asked in 2017.

articles.title: Thomas Crooks trained with long rifle up to the day before he shot at Trump: docs
articles.summary: According to the documents, Crooks registered for the July 13, 2024 rally on July 6 and requested one ticket.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Newly released documents from the investigation into Thomas Matthew Crooks, who attempted to assassinate President Trump in 2024, provide new details about his firearms training before the attack and how people around him said he appeared nonviolent, even as his interest in shooting became more intense.

The docs were part of a large records request filed by various media outlets and included details surrounding how authorities were able to piece together Crooks’ whereabouts.

The records also detail the sprawling investigation, which involved thousands of tips and hundreds of interviews as authorities worked to reconstruct the gunman’s movements and determine a motive .

Authorities spoke to several people who said they either saw or encountered Crooks the day of the shooting. According to the documents, he registered for Trump’s July 13, 2024, rally in Butler, Pa., on July 6 and requested one ticket.

Federal authorities said during the campaign event, he fired several shots at Trump, one of which grazed the top of the then-GOP presidential candidate’s ear.

Crooks killed Pennsylvania firefighter Corey Comperatore and injured two people at that rally before he was taken out by a U.S. Secret Service sniper.

The FBI said its investigation did not establish a definitive motive or uncover credible evidence that Crooks conspired with anyone else.

Investigators also previously disclosed that in the 30 days before the attack, Crooks conducted more than 60 searches related to both Trump and then-President Biden.

Crooks spent significant time at shooting ranges

Records show that Crooks took three paid firearms-training courses in the seven weeks before the assassination attempt , providing new details about the extent of his formal training leading up to the shooting.

The 2024 courses included a basic carbine Course on May 25, a basic handgun course on June 13 and an intermediate handgun course on June 22.

Crooks regularly went to the Clairton Sportsmen’s Club, about once a week, where he would take a rifle and shotgun. Shooting was described as his “new hobby.”

Witnesses told investigators he regularly practiced on targets as far as 100 yards away, and one training course classmate said they were “very impressed” with his marksmanship.

One of his shooting instructors described Crooks as “quiet, stayed to himself, loner, and non-aggressive.”

The records also show his interest becoming more advanced.

Crooks bought ammunition and gun accessories online, including a chest rig and ceramic plates. Additionally, he became interested in rapid-action range-transition shooting, according to the documents.

Crooks described as ‘quiet’ and ‘pleasant’

Despite Crooks’ increasing involvement with firearms, people who knew him described no obvious warning signs, while witnesses offered differing accounts of his political views.

A friend said he “liked to shoot rifles” but had never expressed a desire to harm anyone and was not known to have mental health or substance-abuse problems.

Another person close to Crooks told investigators he “never expressed political views or an interest in explosives” and said his behavior in the days leading up to the shooting did not appear out of the ordinary.

Several names were redacted in the public records.

Someone who worked with Crooks described him as “a pleasant individual” and remembered him as “excelling in the course.”

For a final project, the gunman designed and 3D-printed a Rubik’s Cube with Braille so it could be used by people who are blind. The witness said he “never had any negative interaction with Crooks,” though their contact was limited to the classroom and lab.

He was repeatedly described as an exceptional student with high SAT scores, straight As and perfect attendance.

One person said Crooks was “quiet,” “helpful and friendly,” and said he had never done anything to make them believe “there was an ounce of violence in him.”

He was also described as an isolated student who was bullied and had few disciplinary issues.

The newly released interviews also provide more detail about conflicting recollections of his politics.

One witness said Crooks called himself a Republican and opposed “woke” ideology but did not believe the 2020 election was rigged. A relative also told investigators that the shooter did not believe the 2020 election fraud claims.

Another recalled him removing signs that said, “Keep Trump out of office” and referring to “commies.”

Though none of the accounts describe him as intensely political.

articles.body:
President Trump will rejoin the campaign trail Wednesday evening, traveling to North Carolina to rally support for GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who formerly chaired the Republican National Committee.

Recent polls placed the Republican hopeful behind his Democratic opponent, former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper. Whatley received Trump’s blessing to pursue the Tar Heel State’s open Senate seat back in 2025, after the president’s daughter in law — Lara Trump — decided not to make a bid for the seat.

Whatley also joined other GOP candidates, lawmakers and officials at the party’s inaugural midterm convention last week.

Meanwhile, both chambers of Congress have a schedule packed with hearings as the House prepares for another recess. Lawmakers will hear from officials about a range of national security issues — including the evolution of counterterrorism in the 25 years post-9/11, securing U.S. leadership in the global biotechnology race and competition with China.

The Senate will speak with several nominees Trump tapped for leadership roles across federal public health regulatory agencies. One of these hearings will feature Nicole Saphier, the president’s third nominee for surgeon general.

The Federal Reserve board will address interest rates Wednesday afternoon. The central bank is expected to hike its rates amid rising inflation and the growing economic toll of the Iran war.

articles.title: AI buildout propels tech firms to top of US investment ranking: Study
articles.summary: The rapid buildout of artificial intelligence is making technology firms some of the top capital investors in the U.S., according to new research shared first with The Hill. articles.body:
The rapid buildout of artificial intelligence is making technology firms some of the top capital investors in the U.S., according to new research shared first with The Hill.

The report, to be published by the think tank Progressive Policy Institute (PPI) Wednesday, found tech firms Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft invested more than half — $269 billion — of the $520 billion in U.S. capital spending last year.

Amazon tops this list, with just over $93 million in estimated domestic expenditures last year. Financial and non-health insurance companies were excluded from the analysis.

This marked a 61.1 percent increase from their spending in 2024, with analysts pointing to the increased demand for compute and the infrastructure needed to power AI. Oracle also made the top 10, spending more than $15.7 million in domestic investments.

Michael Mandel, PPI’s chief economist who runs the annual “Investment Heroes” report, told The Hill his team hasn’t “seen any great growth out of the companies that are investing in the AI boom.”

Other top domestic spenders on the list include Walmart, Verizon Communications, AT&T, Apple, Exxon Mobil and Chevron.

When PPI first started this report in 2012, industrial companies — such as those in fiber networks, power grids and retailers — dominated the top of the lists, but over time, the tech firms “just kept rising.”

The utilities, construction and and manufacturing sectors were originally projected to grow in productivity by at least 14 percent from 2016 to 2026, but all three fell by at least 4.5 percent from 2014 to 2024, according to the report.

The information sector, including the Big Tech firms, internet providers and semiconductor firms, was the only to actually grow in productivity, by 61.3 percent, the report states.

PPI acknowledged the backlash facing AI firms and data center hyperscalers, but argued concerns are “manageable.”

“True, data centers can bring real issues like electricity rates, water use, or noise,” the think tank wrote. “Local and state governments have access to a selection of practical tools that minimize impacts and ensure that communities reap the benefits of the investment they host.

“The massive buildout of data centers, chips, transmission, and connectivity are positioning the country for growth and strategic strength.”

Mandel added the AI boom is “the only game in town really” when it comes to boosting productivity and increasing living standards and affordability.

He hopes AI ambitions can revive other sectors, like manufacturing, by generating new jobs and increasing productivity.

“We sort of live in this world in which the digital sector have invested a lot and grown much faster, and the physical sectors … have invested a lot less and grown much more slowly,” Mandel said. “Our task here going forward, if we want to meet the changes, we have to sort of use AI to help accelerate growth in manufacturing.”

“If we were just investing in AI for better chatbots, you can understand [why] people will be troubled by data centers,” he added. “If the data centers are going to be surrounded by sort of high tech manufacturing that can sort of add jobs and reduce costs, it becomes a much more appealing proposition.”

Public sentiment around AI and the firms behind it has plummeted over the past year amid concerns around data centers, the labor workforce and its ability to supercharge bad actors.

A Gallup poll released in July found public confidence in large technology companies was at a record low, dropping from 32 percent in 2020 to 20 percent in 2026.

Market analysts have expressed concerns this year that major tech firms’ AI ambitions are causing these companies to take on massive amounts of debt in the interim.

There has been a massive increase in bonds issued by these hyperscalers, surging from just $16.7 billion in 2024 to $193 billion so far in 2026, according to data from LSEG.

To conduct the study, PPI’s analysts selected the top 200 companies from the Fortune 500 list, removing financial and non-health insurance companies. All of the companies included in the rankings are based in the U.S.; due to data comparability issues, internationally based companies were not included.

Researchers estimated U.S. capital expenditures based on data in companies’ annual 10-K statements and other financial documents.

articles.body:
Former President Obama and his family say they’re mourning the loss of their “pretty much perfect” dog, Sunny.

“Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family,” Obama wrote in a Wednesday post on the social platform X.

The Obamas welcomed Sunny , a 1-year-old Portuguese water dog, in 2013.

“We got Sunny at the start of our second term in the White House, and all of us – including our first dog, Bo – immediately fell in love,” Obama said.

“We also had trouble keeping up with her, for Sunny was a force of nature,” the 44th president said in his tribute to the four-legged family member.

Bo and Sunny often made cameo appearances at the White House during public events and were prominently featured on the family’s annual holiday card. Former first lady Michelle Obama said in 2015 that the pair of pooches was so popular that they had their own official White House schedules.

“Everybody wants to see them and take pictures,” Michelle Obama said at the time.

“I get a memo at the beginning of the month with a request for their schedules, and I have to approve their appearances,” she said.

In his homage to Sunny, the former president remembered the pup as “athletic and full of boundless energy, she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren’t even there, chasing squirrels, birds and anything else that moved.”

“And whereas the way to Bo’s heart usually involved a treat, Sunny was more interested in having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing,” Obama said.

Saying that Sunny loved both his daughters, Sasha and Malia, “even if they were pestering her when she was napping,” Obama remembered the canine would follow members of the family’s staff around “helping them on the job.”

“She was fiercely protective of Bo, who she rightly sensed wasn’t always as alert and attentive as she was,” Obama said.

“She had her eccentricities: other than Bo, she preferred people to dogs; she was a loud and sloppy drinker; and despite being a Portuguese Water Dog, she hated getting wet,” Obama said of Sunny.

“But as far as our family was concerned, she was pretty much perfect, and for 13 years, she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days,” Obama said.

“We will miss her terribly, and imagine she’s with her big brother now, making sure he’s okay.”

articles.title: Patel rips Democrats after clashes at hearing: ‘Buffoons’
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel rebuked Democratic lawmakers who criticized him on Tuesday during an oversight hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, accusing them of acting “like buffoons on Capitol Hill.” “This FBI, under my leadership and President Trump’s administration, is here for the people of America, not for the cacophony of the United States Senate…
articles.body:
FBI Director Kash Patel rebuked Democratic lawmakers who criticized him on Tuesday during an oversight hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, accusing them of acting “like buffoons on Capitol Hill.”

“This FBI, under my leadership and President Trump’s administration, is here for the people of America, not for the cacophony of the United States Senate and the Democrats and their radical lunacy,” the FBI director said during an interview on Fox News’s “Hannity.”

He added, “We are here to protect Americans.”

Democratic lawmakers on the committee pressed Patel over reports that he used taxpayer dollars to fund personal excursions. The FBI director has refuted these accusations , releasing a July letter he sent to Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) in which he pledged he was “fully compliant” with agency rules on Monday.

In one heated exchange with Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) during the Tuesday hearing, the Democrat slammed Patel over the reports and accused him of lying about subpoenaing journalists. Grassley interrupted his colleague during the lengthy questioning, asking the New Jersey lawmaker if he was “ready to shut up.”

Booker was pressing the FBI director over the administration’s decision to subpoena a reporter from The New York Times who wrote a story about Patel’s girlfriend receiving a detail of SWAT agents.

“I have a right to ask questions about how he’s spending money on his girlfriend, and yet he stonewalls me but will run on Fox News and talk about any and all of these issues,” Booker told Grassley.

“This is ridiculous. This is a sham,” he continued. “And what’s bad is not the person sitting there, who’s a mockery to the office he holds. What’s bad is the people that are enabling him to do so.”

Patel has maintained that the subpoenas were targeted at identifying leakers in the FBI who are talking to journalists.

“This administration focuses on the leakers of classified information that endanger the lives of elected officials and American citizens,” the bureau chief told Booker. “We are not targeting reporters at any point in time.”

articles.title: Republicans are feeling sick over the nation’s Trump hangover
articles.summary: By making their party into a giant celebration of Trump, Republicans have tied themselves to every one of Trump’s very public failures.
articles.body:
Last year’s election in Virginia offered early hints that voters were prepared to punish Republicans up and down the ballot for enabling President Trump’s disastrous presidency. Nearly 40 percent of voters told pollsters they cast their votes to oppose Trump, even if they disapproved of the Democratic candidate as well.

In the historic electoral wipeout that followed, Democrats swept every statewide race and flipped more than a dozen seats in the legislature.

Things have only gotten worse for Republicans after a year of inaction in Washington amid skyrocketing gas prices and stubborn inflation.

In Maine, a CNN poll published last week reveals that nearly half of those surveyed view their vote in this year’s Senate race as a chance to oppose Trump’s agenda. A CBS News-YouGov poll published on Sunday found the same trend nationally, where 45 percent said they were voting specifically to oppose Trump.

Half of Americans now use the words “corrupt” and “extreme” to describe Trump’s radicalized Republican Party. Republicans have so badly alienated regular people that voters are actually excited to punish anyone associated with Trump’s failed presidency. I call that voter rage the “Trump hangover effect,” and it is reshaping national races that were once considered reliable Republican strongholds.

Republican strategists weren’t prepared to spend 2026 worrying about Kansas, a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, but Trump Hangover Syndrome is complicating the math even among heartland conservatives. A co/efficient poll released last week found Sen. Roger Marshall (R) led his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton (D) by just 5 points, even though the survey oversampled Republican respondents by 10 points compared to current partisanship models . If Marshall is really underperforming that badly in Kansas, Democrats could enter the final stretch of the midterms with a broader electoral map than even they predicted.

The Trump hangover effect is also on display in Tennessee, where Democrat Justin Pearson (D) narrowly trails Republican Brent Taylor (R) by 4 points in the state’s redrawn 9th Congressional District. Trump won the newly constituted district by 20 points in 2024. Pearson is no doubt helped by the fact that Trump’s popularity has cratered to a net minus-3 rating among Tennesseans, with high gas prices and affordability issues driving voters’ negative feelings.

In fact, Trump’s unpopularity nationwide is staggering in its consistency. Kansans give Trump a minus-17 approval rating , his lowest-ever in the state, which concerned Republicans enough that they dispatched Vice President JD Vance to try and bolster Marshall’s flatlining campaign. Marshall also distanced himself from Trump’s increasingly toxic presidency this week by backtracking on his support for Trump’s dubious promise to issue $5,000 checks to every American if Republicans win the midterms.

Most of Trump’s unpopularity comes from his inability to slow the surging price of oil , which just surpassed $100 per barrel for the first time since May, but Republicans aren’t being helped by the total incoherence of their party’s message on oil prices.

Last Sunday, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) admitted on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that gas prices and inflation were “ gutting people like a fish ” and that a dysfunctional Republican Congress had the power — but not the political will — to address inflation before the election. Two days later, Fox News host Laura Ingraham made the exact opposite argument. She that gas prices were actually decreasing . One day after Ingraham’s remarks, Trump acknowledged the high price of gas but told voters that high prices were the necessary cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb.

Faced with a crisis they created and yet can’t seem to fix, Republicans are saying everything — and as a result, voters are hearing nothing. Americans across party lines now tell pollsters they feel Trump has failed on the economy, with just 35 percent of Americans approving of his job performance in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll. The man who claimed he could fix everything has actually made everything worse, and voters are sick of waiting for solutions they no longer believe Republicans are capable of delivering.

By making their party into a giant celebration of Trump, Republicans have tied themselves to every one of his very public failures. If Republicans thought the drubbings they got in New Jersey and Virginia last year were catastrophic, wait until they meet voters who are even angrier at Trump today than they were a year ago.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: Dem House speaker torched for invoking 9/11 to attack key Trump policy: 'Totally wrong'
articles.summary: Ryan Mackenzie demands Joanna McClinton apologize after the Pennsylvania House Speaker linked Trump's immigration crackdown to potential 9/11 violence.
articles.body: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, R-Pa., fired back at the Pennsylvania House speaker, a Democrat, after she suggested the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration could invite 9/11-like violence. "She used her time to actually denounce securing our border and saying that, somehow, the efforts to keep our country safe could lead to another attack," Mackenzie told Fox News Digital. "She’s totally wrong. She’s answering to the far-left radicals and globalists. I would actually call on Joanna McClinton to apologize for what she said at that event," he added. McClinton’s criticism highlights a challenge Democrats face as they search for vulnerabilities in Trump’s immigration agenda: attacking the administration’s aggressive enforcement tactics even as illegal border crossings have fallen sharply. DEM REP SETH MOULTON SAYS PARTY HAS NO IMMIGRATION PLAN, IS ONLY ‘OPPOSITION TO TRUMP’ Speaking at a panel discussion on the 250th anniversary of American independence, McClinton said she feared the threat of retaliation for Trump’s "brutality." "When we think of just the brutality of this federal government for almost two years, it’s been heartless. It’s been too silent on the other side of the aisle. They are treating people with no respect or dignity — people who came here to do better. It’s horrible. So, when we think about where we are in 2026 and that it’s been 25 years, thank God we have not had another attack," McClinton said. "Thank God we haven’t seen another plane go down in Pennsylvania. But we also have to recognize that our policies are impacting our perception around the world," McClinton added. McClinton first became speaker in the Pennsylvania House in 2023 and first joined the chamber in 2015. Before her time in politics, she worked as a public defender. McClinton has voiced similar criticisms of immigration enforcement before, framing Trump’s use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as a tool that has gone too far. DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE "On our 250th birthday we’re seeing the worst horrors unfold in our beloved nation!!! Completely horrified by ICE agents so brutally hunting down, harming people every day – and now using deadly force!!!! God have mercy," McClinton wrote in a post to X, referring to deadly encounters between ICE and protesters earlier this year. Since Trump returned to office, illegal border crossings have sunk to historic lows. Since the end of 2024, encounters have gone from 144,000 in December 2024 to just 33,800 in July — a reduction of 76.5%. Mackenzie believes Democrats like McClinton are ignoring that record. "What she should be doing is making sure that we’re protecting and defending American citizens in our country at every single turn," Mackenzie said. SHAPIRO VS TRUMP-BACKED GARRITY SET FOR HIGH-STAKES PENNSYLVANIA GOVERNOR SHOWDOWN In addition to demanding an apology from McClinton, Mackenzie also called on other Democrats, like his own congressional opponent, to condemn her thinking. "My opponent in the congressional race, Bob Brooks, should condemn that kind of rhetoric. We need to make sure that we are always pushing back on these types of things that are really inappropriate and being said by Democrat leaders who are trying to push their radical agenda instead of doing what is right for our country," Mackenzie said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP McClinton’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.body:
Kerry Kennedy, the sister of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., blamed President Trump for the Kennedy Center’s board voting to close the performing arts venue, calling the decision a “tragedy”

“The American people love the Kennedy Center,” she told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Tuesday. “They love the arts. They understand what’s going on, they see the corruption of this.”

The Trump-aligned board voted to close the center for renovations, with officials claiming it faces “fiscal collapse.” The trustees also cited a recent water leak that caused damage to the grand foyer ceiling as proof the building is “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

But Kerry Kennedy, the daughter of former Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, said the center is not facing a “financial issue.”

“President Trump has said they have $250 million, ready to hand over tomorrow,” she continued, referring to the building’s congressionally appropriated funding.

“He’s just withholding it because he wants his name on the building,” Kerry Kennedy added. “So, this is like so many other things that Trump has touched. It’s a bankruptcy because he adds his name to it.”

Minutes before the Kennedy Center board’s vote to close the facility, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper again blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to add the president’s name to the building’s exterior.

After Cooper’s ruling, Trump warned the center will not be renovated if judges continue to shut down the name change.

Kerry Kennedy was not the only family member to knock the president over the closure.

Her cousin, Maria Shriver, said the fact that “a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building” was a “sad state of affairs.”

Shriver’s mother, Eunice Kennedy Shriver, was the sister of former President Kennedy and the late attorney general.

“Actually, how small minded, how narcissistic,” Shriver wrote Tuesday on social platform X. “Actually great men, devoted to public service and the public good do not act like this.”

articles.title: AI is finally making us question our bias in favor of deregulation
articles.summary: On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging tech leaders to slow the pace of AI development. On a Sunday CBS News interview, he added that it “could be a good idea” to have an AI kill switch — not unlike what Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) have proposed. “Some…
articles.body:
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging tech leaders to slow the pace of AI development.

On a Sunday CBS News interview , he added that it “could be a good idea” to have an AI kill switch — not unlike what Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) have proposed . “Some kind of oversight, some kind of joint governance,” he argued, is needed to stave off “great risks” to the public, including “losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption.”

Somewhat astonishingly, rival tech billionaires Sam Altman and Elon Musk swiftly backed Amodei’s warning : “Dario is right,” Musk posted on X.

What Amodei, Altman and Musk are saying, loudly and clearly, is that there is a vital role for government regulation when it comes to AI. Since the 1970s, however, Republicans and many leading Democrats have pushed deregulation as a priority. Republicans have especially preached that that “ the role of the federal government should be limited ,” and that Congress should take aggressive steps to “alleviate federal regulatory and bureaucratic burdens on individuals and businesses.”

Deregulation has broadly been achieved across numerous industries, including banking, energy, labor, the environment, and telecommunications. The underlying economic argument is that deregulation enables businesses to hire and spend more, increasing productivity and ultimately lowering costs for consumers. Trump’s 2025 AI Action Plan explicitly emphasized removing regulatory obstacles to AI development and infrastructure.

Meanwhile, federal income-tax rates on businesses have fallen substantially over the same period on a similar rationale: that lower tax burdens encourage investment and economic growth. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act cut the top individual income-tax rate from 70 percent to 50 percent. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, passed during President Trump’s first term, reduced the federal corporate income-tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent.

What has been missing from the debates over deregulation and tax-cuts is a basic recognition that regulation provides crucial public benefits that businesses are not incentivized to provide or pay for on their own — for example, cleaner air, safer workplaces, financial stability and consumer protection.

“My view here,” Amodei told CBS, “is it has always been very strange that this technology is being built by a private company. People ask me that question all the time — why isn’t this being built by government. And the strangest thing about it is, I agree with them, I’m uncomfortable.”

Yet in countless other ways, the Trump administration has increasingly fused public power with private enterprise. As part of his ramped-up ICE crackdown, for example, he has massively expanded the reach of private prison companies. Their 2025 revenue estimate is pegged at about $5.5 billion, $2.4 billion of which came from ICE alone.

Trump has also brokered numerous public-private financial deals with taxpayer money, such as a $620 million loan to Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet company tied to Donald Trump, Jr. The federal government is now a partial owner in companies such as Intel , in which Trump made an $8.9 billion investment of federal dollars in exchange for a 9.9 percent equity stake . Just this month, the Pentagon acquired a 35 percent equity position in North American Blue Energy Partners , giving the U.S. government an ownership interest in a company involved in Venezuelan oil production.

The federal government is thus using private companies to achieve public objectives — including becoming a shareholder in major private companies whose bottom lines depend on favorable federal regulation and investment.

This is not how American government is supposed to work. With rare exceptions , the Constitution does not bind private conduct, on the theory that the government requires specialized constraints due to its uniquely coercive and monetary powers. That public-private power structure is radically changing.

All the while, the Republican Party continues to pretend that corporations and the market have all the answers to the public’s problems. Let them do their thing and everything will work out well, the theory goes, including for the average American worker.

It’s increasingly clear that the bountiful mantra of deregulation and tax-cutting for corporations is a myth. Or worse, a deliberate lie. Said Amodei: “I think for too long the industry lied to people about the fact that this technology had risks.”

But who can really blame corporations? Under the influential laws of Delaware , directors of for-profit corporations are restrained from adopting business strategies that deliberately reject shareholder wealth maximization in favor of unrelated social objectives. The government’s job is exactly the opposite.

Members of Congress, federal judges, and the president all take an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution and, in effect, its underlying values — including “justice,” “domestic tranquility,” “the general welfare,” and the “blessings of liberty.” If it takes AI to get voters to demand a government for the people — not for corporations — maybe that’s a good thing. November will tell.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: Abbott orders penalties for Texas data centers that fail to report water use
articles.summary: The governor’s office said that some major water users, including data centers, appear to have violated state law by failing to provide required information about their water use.
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas (KXAN) — Gov. Greg Abbott (R) said this week he is directing the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that fail to enforce state water-use reporting requirements.

The governor’s office said that some major water users, including data centers, appear to have violated state law by failing to provide required information about their water use. Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to impose legal consequences for past and future reporting failures.

“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water. The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. I direct the Texas Water Development Board to use its enforcement authority to penalize past failures and to impose legal consequences for any future failure to comply,” Abbott said in a statement.

Under the Texas Water Code, recipients of a TWDB water-use survey are required to complete and return it. According to Abbott’s office, a data center that fails to do so could face criminal consequences and become ineligible for certain Texas Commission on Environmental Quality permits, amendments or renewals. TWDB can also refer noncompliance to the appropriate county or district attorney.

KXAN reached out to the Texas water Development Board for comment on the directive, in a statement they said:

“ The TWDB recognizes the need for complete water-use reporting from major water users, including data centers. Those reports are critical to the agency’s long-term water planning. At the direction of Governor Abbott, the TWDB will compel all water users to comply with Texas Water Code survey requirements so that the State has the information it needs to plan for Texas’ future water needs. “

Democratic gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa also criticized Abbott’s directive.

In a statement to KXAN, Hinojosa said Texans need stronger regulations governing data centers and called on Abbott to call a special session. In a statement she said:

“Looks like Greg Abbott saw another bad poll today. A strongly worded letter every day from now until the election won’t change Texans’ minds about how Abbott has made Texas the Wild West of data centers, raked in $20 million in donations from their CEOs, and pledged to make Texas the ‘epicenter’ of AI at the expense of working people. Texans deserve real regulations on data centers right now, and unless Abbott calls a special session to pass laws that protect Texans and give them a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities – as I called for months ago – this is all just more lip service to save his campaign.”

Some Texans who have pushed back against data center development also say the governor’s directive does not go far enough.

Claudia Hollern, a volunteer with the Caldwell Data Center Action Team, said she believes the state should consider broader action.

“At this point, it seems like, kind of a distraction instead of an actual directive to make these data centers slow down. I don’t understand why Greg Abbott doesn’t just call a special session and have a moratorium to pause this,” said Claudia Hollern, a volunteer with the Caldwell Data Center Action Team.

In August, Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas to conduct a comprehensive audit of data centers that advance through ERCOT’s interconnection process.

That audit includes information about water consumption, water sources and the use of water-efficient technologies. Data center projects that fail to complete the audit process are required to be denied interconnection, according to the governor’s office.

TWDB will work with ERCOT as part of that effort to gather additional information about data center water use.

The agency is required to provide Abbott with an update on the progress of its enforcement efforts by Oct. 14.

Tom Seng, an Assistant Professor of Energy Finance at Texas Christian University, said he was surprised the state had not already taken stronger enforcement action.

“I think water is rising to the top in terms of critical issues. We have ways to produce electricity, I don’t know that we have ways to produce fresh drinking water. Going forward, we need to have a set of rules and standards. I’m a little surprised that this hasn’t already been going on,” said Seng.
